claims.text: Dynamic strain aging governs the dynamic mechanical response of solidified FeNiCrMn.
Dynamic strain aging in FeNiCrMn involves intermittent pinning of moving dislocations by solute atoms.
Cr and Mn are the primary solutes responsible for dislocation pinning in FeNiCrMn.
Pinned dislocations thermally activate and unpin.
The proposed pinning and unpinning mechanism causes serrated plastic flow.
The proposed mechanism causes temperature- and strain-rate-dependent yield behavior.
At lower temperatures, thermally activated dislocation glide is hindered by solute pinning.
At higher strain rates, dislocation glide is hindered by solute pinning.
Intermittent dislocation-unpinning events manifest as serrations in stress–strain curves.
Higher temperatures reduce the solute-pinning effect through thermal activation.
Reduced solute pinning at higher temperatures produces smoother plastic flow.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit serrated flow at intermediate temperatures and high strain rates.
At higher temperatures, FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower dynamic yield strength.
At room temperature and moderate strain rate, FeNiCrMn has a strength–ductility balance similar to Co-containing counterparts.
The proposed mechanism is expected to govern only homogeneous, solidified FeNiCrMn without significant secondary phases or defect clusters.
The proposed mechanism is limited to uniaxial loading regimes.
Highly cracked or voided FeNiCrMn may not exhibit the proposed response.
The controlled study will vary temperature from approximately 77 K to 500 K and strain rate from 10^-4 s^-1 to 1 s^-1.
The exact temperature and strain-rate thresholds for onset or suppression of serrated flow are uncertain.
Absence of the expected serrated flow or absence of microscopic evidence for solute-induced pinning and unpinning would falsify DSA as the sole controlling mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism associates serrated flow with lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, whereas the predicted outcome places it at intermediate temperatures and high strain rates. The lower-versus-intermediate temperature regime is not reconciled.
